body:
What are biopharmaceuticals?

Many medicines are manufactured by combining chemicals through a series of reactions. Biotechnology provides another method: living cells or biological systems can produce substances that prevent, diagnose or treat diseases. Medicines obtained through such biological processes are called biopharmaceuticals or biological medicines.

Biopharmaceuticals include therapeutic proteins, certain hormones, monoclonal antibodies and some other biological products. Vaccines are also biological products, although their principal purpose is usually to prevent disease rather than treat an existing illness.

Biopharmaceutical: A medicinal product manufactured using a biological source or process, such as living cells, microorganisms or their components.

Why proteins are important medicines

Proteins are chains of amino acids folded into particular shapes. Their structures allow them to perform specific functions. Enzymes accelerate chemical reactions, hormones transmit messages, antibodies recognise particular targets, and some proteins help blood clot.

A disease may develop because an essential protein is absent, insufficient, defective or acting abnormally. Biotechnology can help by supplying a useful protein or by producing an antibody that acts on a disease-related target.

For example, insulin regulates blood glucose. People who require insulin treatment can receive manufactured insulin. An antibody medicine, by contrast, may recognise a particular protein on a cancer cell and interfere with its activity.

What makes a protein recombinant?

A gene is a segment of DNA containing information used to produce a functional product, often a protein. In ordinary cellular protein production, information from DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA, and the RNA is translated into a chain of amino acids.

Recombinant DNA technology allows scientists to place a selected gene into a suitable host cell. The cell then uses the genetic information to produce the desired protein. A protein produced through expression of such an introduced gene is called a recombinant protein.

The host may be a bacterium, yeast or an animal cell. The choice depends partly on the structure and processing requirements of the protein. Some complex human proteins need modifications that certain bacterial cells cannot perform correctly.

From a useful gene to a medicine

The main stages of recombinant protein production can be understood without studying laboratory procedures:

  1. Identify the useful gene: Determine which genetic information is needed to produce the required protein.
  2. Introduce the gene into a suitable host: The selected host cell receives the genetic instructions.
  3. Produce the protein: The host cells use those instructions to manufacture the protein.
  4. Recover and purify the product: The desired protein is separated from cells and unwanted substances.
  5. Check and formulate the medicine: Its identity, purity, biological activity, safety and stability must satisfy applicable quality requirements.

Production in living cells does not automatically make a medicine safe. The final product must undergo appropriate evaluation and quality control.

Biopharmaceuticals and ordinary chemical medicines

Many conventional medicines contain comparatively small molecules with well-defined chemical structures. Biological medicines often contain larger and more complex molecules. Their properties can be affected by the living production system and manufacturing conditions.

This difference is important when comparing generic medicines and biosimilars. A generic version of a conventional small-molecule medicine normally contains the same active chemical substance as its reference medicine. A biosimilar is a biological medicine shown to be highly similar to an approved reference biological medicine, without clinically meaningful differences in safety and effectiveness under the applicable regulatory standard.

Recombinant describes how a product is made using introduced genetic information. Therapeutic describes its medical purpose. A recombinant protein may be a treatment, a vaccine antigen or another useful product.

Prelims focus

  • DNA contains genetic information; messenger RNA carries instructions for protein synthesis.
  • Recombinant proteins are produced by host cells expressing introduced genetic information.
  • Bacteria, yeast and animal cells can be used as production hosts.
  • Biopharmaceuticals include recombinant hormones and monoclonal antibodies.
  • A biosimilar must demonstrate high similarity to a reference biological medicine.
  • Trap: A biological medicine is not necessarily a vaccine, and recombinant production does not eliminate the need for safety testing.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XI, Chapter 9, Biomolecules; NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 6, Molecular Basis of Inheritance, sections on transcription and translation; Chapter 11, Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, sections 11.1 and 11.3; US Food and Drug Administration, Biosimilars Basics for Patients, sections What is a biosimilar medication? and Biosimilar versus generic medicines, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Biopharmaceuticals: How Living Cells Produce Medicines

body:
Replacing a missing or insufficient protein

Some diseases can be treated by supplying a protein that the patient's body does not produce in sufficient quantity or cannot use properly. Such proteins may replace a natural substance, correct a deficiency or perform a specific biological function.

Recombinant human insulin is an important example. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas. It helps regulate the concentration of glucose in blood. People with type 1 diabetes require insulin because their bodies cannot produce enough of it. Some people with type 2 diabetes also need insulin treatment.

How recombinant insulin differs from earlier animal-derived insulin

Before recombinant insulin became available, insulin for medical use was commonly extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs. These animal-derived preparations helped treat diabetes, but differences between animal and human insulin and limitations of supply created disadvantages.

Recombinant DNA technology made it possible to produce human insulin using genetically modified microorganisms. In a historically important development, Eli Lilly produced recombinant human insulin using bacteria in 1983, as described in the Class XII biotechnology textbook.

Mature human insulin contains 2 polypeptide chains, A and B, joined by disulphide bonds. In the human body, insulin is initially made as a precursor called proinsulin. This precursor contains an additional connecting portion called the C-peptide, which is removed when mature insulin is formed.

The early recombinant method described in NCERT involved producing the A and B chains separately in bacterial cells and then combining them to obtain functional human insulin. Modern production methods may differ, but the essential biological distinction remains: mature insulin does not contain the C-peptide.

Insulin is a protein hormone. Ordinary oral administration would expose unprotected insulin to digestive processes, so standard insulin treatment is generally given by injection or through an insulin-delivery device. Not every therapeutic protein can be administered as an ordinary tablet.

Other medically useful recombinant proteins

Recombinant proteinNormal biological roleMedical application
Human insulinRegulates blood glucoseInsulin treatment in diabetes
ErythropoietinStimulates red blood cell productionSelected forms of anaemia, including some cases associated with chronic kidney disease
Factor VIIIParticipates in blood clottingReplacement treatment for haemophilia A
Human growth hormoneSupports growth and developmentSelected conditions involving growth hormone deficiency

These examples show that recombinant proteins do not all perform the same function. Insulin is a hormone, erythropoietin supports blood cell production, and factor VIII participates in coagulation. Matching the protein to its biological role is more useful than memorising a list without understanding it.

Why production quality matters

A useful protein must have an appropriate structure and activity. Manufacturing therefore involves careful purification, examination of contaminants, testing of potency and checking whether the final preparation remains stable during storage.

Some proteins may also trigger an unwanted immune response; the ability to elicit an immune response is called immunogenicity. Recombinant human proteins can reduce certain problems associated with proteins obtained from another species, but no biological medicine is automatically free from adverse reactions.

Therapeutic proteins and vaccine antigens are different uses of recombinant production

A recombinant protein given to restore a missing body function is a therapeutic protein. A recombinant protein that represents part of a disease-causing organism may instead be used as a vaccine antigen, stimulating the immune system to develop protection.

For example, recombinant human insulin is administered to help control diabetes. The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine contains a viral surface antigen that stimulates immunity against hepatitis B; it does not supply insulin or directly treat diabetes.

Prelims focus

  • Insulin is produced naturally by pancreatic beta cells.
  • Mature insulin contains A and B polypeptide chains connected by disulphide bonds.
  • The C-peptide is present in proinsulin but absent from mature insulin.
  • Recombinant human insulin was developed as an alternative to animal-derived insulin.
  • Factor VIII is associated with haemophilia A; erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell production.
  • Trap: Recombinant production describes the manufacturing method, not whether a protein acts as a treatment or a vaccine antigen.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, section 12.2.1, Genetically Engineered Insulin; Chapter 11, Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, sections 11.3.5 and 11.3.6; NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, section 8.2.4, Vaccination and Immunisation.]

title: Recombinant Therapeutic Proteins: Insulin, Blood Factors and Other Examples

body:
Antibodies and their targets

An antibody is a protein produced by specialised immune cells in response to a particular foreign substance or other recognised target. The substance recognised by an antibody is called an antigen.

An antibody binds to a particular region of its target, called an epitope. This specificity is important because an antibody directed against one antigen does not necessarily bind to an unrelated antigen.

Antibodies normally arise as part of acquired immunity. B lymphocytes can develop into plasma cells that release antibodies. T lymphocytes have different immune functions, including supporting immune responses and recognising infected or abnormal cells.

Monoclonal and polyclonal antibodies

During an ordinary immune response, several different B-cell populations may recognise different parts of an antigen. The resulting mixture is described as polyclonal antibodies.

A monoclonal antibody is a preparation of highly uniform antibodies derived from one selected antibody-producing cell lineage. The antibodies recognise the same specific target region. This property makes monoclonal antibodies useful in diagnosis and targeted treatment.

FeatureMonoclonal antibodiesPolyclonal antibodies
OriginOne selected antibody-producing cell lineageSeveral antibody-producing cell lineages
Target recognitionOne selected epitopeDifferent epitopes on an antigen may be recognised
CompositionHighly uniform antibody preparationMixture of antibodies
Typical advantageConsistent recognition of a defined targetBroader recognition of an antigen

How monoclonal antibodies are used

Monoclonal antibodies can act in several ways. Depending on the medicine and disease, they may block an unwanted signal, prevent a molecule from attaching to its receptor, neutralise a harmful substance or help immune mechanisms act against particular cells.

One important application is targeted cancer treatment. Some cancer cells produce unusually large quantities of particular proteins that support their growth. A medicine designed to recognise such a protein may work better in tumours that contain the relevant target.

The HER2 and trastuzumab example

HER2 is a protein involved in signals that influence cell growth. Certain breast cancers have excessive HER2 protein expression. These cancers are described as HER2-positive when the relevant tests meet established clinical criteria.

Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets HER2. Its use in suitable patients illustrates the connection between a diagnostic biomarker and a targeted medicine. Testing for the target helps determine whether a HER2-directed treatment is appropriate.

Trastuzumab is not a general treatment for every form of breast cancer. Other clinical characteristics and treatment criteria also matter.

Antibodies used as medicines do not act like vaccines

When a patient receives a manufactured monoclonal antibody, the treatment supplies a ready-made antibody. The patient does not first have to produce that same antibody through vaccination. This is a form of passive immunotherapy.

A vaccine works differently: it exposes the immune system to an antigen or genetic instructions for producing an antigen, encouraging the body to develop its own immune response and often immune memory.

The effect of a monoclonal antibody generally lasts only while sufficient active medicine remains in the body. It does not, merely by being administered, establish the immune memory associated with successful vaccination.

Limitations

Monoclonal antibodies require careful manufacturing and quality control. They can be expensive, may require repeated doses, and can cause adverse effects. The presence of a target may support treatment selection, but it does not guarantee that every patient will respond.

Prelims focus

  • An antigen is recognised by an antibody; an epitope is the particular region recognised.
  • Monoclonal antibodies originate from one selected antibody-producing cell lineage.
  • Polyclonal antibodies are a mixture produced by different cell lineages.
  • Trastuzumab targets HER2 and is used in selected HER2-positive cancers.
  • Administering ready-made antibodies is not the same as stimulating active immunity through vaccination.
  • Trap: The presence of a cancer diagnosis alone does not establish eligibility for every targeted antibody medicine.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, section 8.2.2, Acquired Immunity; World Health Organization, Monoclonal antibodies, WHO biological standardisation information; US National Cancer Institute, Trastuzumab, Drug Information Summary, and Biomarker Testing for Cancer Treatment, sections on treatment selection, consulted 13 November 2026.]
